activities.title: Core Mechanics: Method Overloading
activities.content:
### What is Method Overloading?

In Java, **Method Overloading** allows a class to have multiple methods with the **exact same name**, as long as their parameter lists are different.

You already rely on method overloading every day:
- `System.out.println(10);`       // calls println(int)
- `System.out.println(3.14);`     // calls println(double)
- `System.out.println("Hello");`  // calls println(String)
- `System.out.println(true);`     // calls println(boolean)

Imagine if Java forced you to remember: `printInt()`, `printDouble()`, `printString()`, and `printBoolean()`! Overloading creates clean, intuitive APIs.

### The Three Valid Overloading Rules

To legally overload a method, the parameter list must differ in at least one of these ways:

1. **Different Number of Parameters (Arity)**:
   ```java
   public static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
   public static int add(int a, int b, int c) { return a + b + c; }
   ```
2. **Different Data Types of Parameters**:
   ```java
   public static double add(double a, double b) { return a + b; }
   ```
3. **Different Order of Parameter Types**:
   ```java
   public static void display(String label, int count) { ... }
   public static void display(int count, String label) { ... }
   ```

### The Cardinal Rule: Return Type ALONE Cannot Overload!

This is one of the most frequently tested interview questions in Java:
```java
// ILLEGAL - WILL NOT COMPILE!
public static int getScore() { return 100; }
public static double getScore() { return 100.0; }
```

Why does this fail?
Remember: the **Method Signature** is only `MethodName + Parameter Types`.
Both methods above have the signature `getScore()`.

If a caller writes:
`getScore();` // (discarding the return value)
How could the compiler know which method you intended to call? It cannot! Therefore, **changing only the return type is a compile-time error**.

### Compile-Time Polymorphism

Method overloading is an example of **Compile-Time Polymorphism** (or Static Binding). The Java compiler inspects the arguments at the call site and binds the call to the exact matching method signature during compilation, with zero runtime overhead.

activities.title: Verified Java Implementation: Method Overloading
activities.description: Trace how the compiler selects between overloaded methods based on argument types and count.

questions.prompt: What allows two methods in the same class to share the same name in Java?
options: They must have different return types
They must have different parameter lists (count, types, or order)
They must have different access modifiers
They must be in different packages
questions.explanation: Method overloading requires different parameter lists (different number, types, or sequence of parameter types).

questions.prompt: Why does 'int compute(int x)' and 'double compute(int x)' fail to compile in the same class?
options: Because double cannot follow int
Because changing only the return type does not change the method signature, causing duplicate method error
Because compute is a reserved keyword
Because static methods cannot return double
questions.explanation: The signature consists strictly of name and parameter types. Both have signature compute(int), which causes a duplicate method collision.

questions.prompt: When does Java resolve which overloaded method to invoke?
options: At compile time (Static Binding)
At runtime (Dynamic Dispatch)
When the Garbage Collector runs
When the operating system boots
questions.explanation: Method overloading is resolved at compile time by matching argument types against available signatures (Compile-Time Polymorphism).

questions.prompt: Given methods: 'void test(int a)' and 'void test(double a)'. Which method is invoked by 'test(5)'?
options: test(double a) because double is wider
test(int a) because 5 is an exact int literal match
A compiler error occurs due to ambiguity
Neither executes
questions.explanation: Java always selects the most specific exact match available. Since 5 is an int literal, test(int a) is selected.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a valid method overload for 'public static void print(String msg)'?
options: public static int print(String msg)
public static void print(String text)
public static void print(String msg, int copies)
private static void print(String msg)
questions.explanation: Option C adds a second parameter (int copies), creating a new distinct signature print(String, int). The others only change return type, parameter name, or access modifier.

questions.prompt: Can methods be overloaded by changing only the parameter variable names, e.g. 'doStuff(int x)' vs 'doStuff(int y)'?
options: Yes, different names create different methods
No, parameter names are ignored by the compiler when matching signatures
Only if names have different lengths
Only in interface declarations
questions.explanation: The compiler matches by data type, not by variable identifier names. (int x) and (int y) are identical signatures.

questions.prompt: What is the common real-world use case for method overloading?
options: To simulate default arguments and provide convenient APIs for varying input types
To make code harder to reverse-engineer
To speed up the JVM bytecode verifier
To avoid using loops
questions.explanation: Overloading allows intuitive API design, providing sensible defaults or accepting diverse data types under a single unified name.

questions.prompt: What error occurs if the compiler finds two equally valid widened matches for an overloaded call, such as 'test(10, 20)' with 'test(int, double)' and 'test(double, int)'?
options: Java picks the first one listed in the file
Compile-time error: 'reference to test is ambiguous'
Java runs both methods in parallel
Runtime NullPointerException
questions.explanation: When two overloaded methods are equally matched through widening conversions, the compiler halts with an ambiguous method call error.

practice.title: Overloaded Multiplier for Two and Three Integers
practice.problemStatement: Write two overloaded static methods named 'multiply': one that takes two ints and returns their product, and one that takes three ints and returns their product. In main(), compute and print multiply(4, 5) and multiply(2, 3, 4).
hints: Second method returns a * b * c.

interviewQA.question: What is Method Overloading and why is it called Compile-Time Polymorphism?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Method Overloading allows defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists. It is called Compile-Time Polymorphism (or static polymorphism) because the compiler decides which specific overloaded method to invoke during compilation based on the static types of the arguments.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Can two methods be overloaded by changing only their return types?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No. The return type is not part of the method signature. If two methods differ only by return type, the compiler cannot disambiguate call sites where the return value is discarded, resulting in a duplicate method compile error.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: How does Java choose an overloaded method when widening conversions are possible?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java follows a strict resolution precedence order: 1) Exact match, 2) Primitive widening conversion (e.g. byte -> short -> int -> long -> float -> double), 3) Autoboxing/unboxing (e.g. int -> Integer), and 4) Varargs. If two methods match at the same precedence level without one being strictly more specific, an ambiguous method error occurs.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Can main() method be overloaded in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes! You can define overloaded versions of main (e.g. main(int x), main(String a, String b)). However, the JVM will strictly execute 'public static void main(String[] args)' as the program entry point. The overloaded versions can be called manually by your code.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between Method Overloading and Method Overriding?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Overloading occurs within the same class (or across subclass hierarchy) where methods share the same name but have DIFFERENT parameter lists; it is resolved at compile time. Overriding occurs between a superclass and subclass where a method has the EXACT SAME signature and return type; it is resolved at runtime based on the actual object instance (dynamic dispatch).
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: Can we overload static methods in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes. Static methods can be overloaded just like instance methods, as long as their parameter lists differ.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

interviewQA.question: How is method forwarding (telescoping) used with method overloading?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Method forwarding is a design pattern where overloaded methods with fewer parameters supply default values and delegate directly to the most comprehensive overloaded method. This avoids duplicate implementation logic and ensures single-point maintenance.
keyPoints: Focus on memory lifecycle and compile-time contract enforcement.

activities.title: Self-Mastery Checklist
checklist: Method Overloading: Multiple methods sharing the same name but with different parameter lists (count, types, or order).
Compile-Time Resolution: The compiler determines which method to call at compile time based on argument types.
Signature Rules: Return types and access modifiers alone CANNOT distinguish overloaded methods.
Default Argument Pattern: Overloaded methods can forward calls with default values to a central implementation.
Overloading vs Overriding: Overloading = different signatures at compile time; Overriding = identical signatures at runtime.
